content: Acetylcysteine, when administered orally, is an amino acid approved by the FDA for the prevention of liver damage that may occur following the ingestion of a potentially hepatotoxic dose of acetaminophen. Common side effects include itching, rash, hives, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. For adults, acetylcysteine is indicated as an antidote to prevent or reduce liver injury after an acetaminophen overdose. Treatment should begin as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of ingestion. Regardless of the reported amount of acetaminophen ingested, acetylcysteine should be administered immediately if less than 24 hours have passed since the overdose. Do not wait for acetaminophen level assay results before starting treatment. The recommended procedures include promptly emptying the stomach via lavage or inducing vomiting with syrup of ipecac. Syrup of ipecac should be given in a dose of 15 mL for children up to age 12 and 30 mL for adolescents and adults, followed by drinking large amounts of water. If vomiting does not occur within 20 minutes, the dose should be repeated. In cases of mixed drug overdose, activated charcoal may be indicated. However, if activated charcoal has been administered, lavage should be performed before starting acetylcysteine treatment, as activated charcoal can adsorb acetylcysteine and reduce its effectiveness. Blood should be drawn for pre-detoxification acetaminophen plasma assay and baseline liver function tests (SGOT, SGPT), bilirubin, prothrombin time, creatinine, BUN, blood sugar, and electrolytes. The loading dose of acetylcysteine is 140 mg per kg of body weight, prepared for oral administration as described in the dosage guide. Subsequent actions should be determined based on pre-detoxification plasma acetaminophen levels. There is limited information regarding off-label uses of oral acetylcysteine in adults, both guideline-supported and non-guideline-supported. Similarly, there is limited information on its FDA-labeled and off-label use in pediatric patients. There are no contraindications to the oral administration of acetylcysteine for treating acetaminophen overdose. However, generalized hives have been rarely observed in patients receiving oral acetylcysteine. If this or other allergic symptoms occur, treatment should be discontinued unless deemed essential and the allergic symptoms can be otherwise controlled. If hepatic failure with encephalopathy becomes evident, acetylcysteine treatment should be stopped to avoid further administration of nitrogenous substances. While there is no evidence that acetylcysteine influences hepatic failure, this remains a theoretical possibility. Oral administration of acetylcysteine, especially in the large doses required for acetaminophen overdose treatment, may cause nausea, vomiting, and other gastrointestinal symptoms. Rash, with or without mild fever, has been rarely observed. There is limited information on drug interactions, use during pregnancy, labor and delivery, nursing mothers, pediatric patients, geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, renal impairment, hepatic impairment, and immunocompromised patients. Acetylcysteine is available in sterile solutions for inhalation (as a mucolytic agent) or oral administration (as an acetaminophen antidote). It is not intended for parenteral injection. The 20% solution (200 mg/mL) can be diluted, while the 10% solution (100 mg/mL) may be used undiluted. Unopened vials should be stored at controlled room temperature (20°-25°C or 68°-77°F). Dilutions should be freshly prepared and used within one hour. If only a portion of the solution is used, the remaining undiluted portion should be refrigerated and used within 96 hours. A change in color after opening does not affect the drug's efficacy. There is no established interaction between alcohol and acetylcysteine, but patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while taking this medication.
